title: Keeping small-group members: why they leave and what to do
audience: Owners and coaches who run membership groups and want to reduce attrition
learningOutcomes: Classify reasons clients leave as controllable or outside the business's control
Set check-ins that catch dissatisfaction early
Use the member's original goal to guide retention actions

instruction.heading: Clients leave for predictable reasons
instruction.body: Small-group members leave for a range of reasons. Some are outside your control, such as moving house or a change in work hours. Others come from the service itself: the member does not feel they fit the group, the coaching feels thin, or the sessions do not match the goal. Some reasons are unclear, and a short exit conversation can help. Sorting reasons this way shows where effort will change outcomes.

instruction.heading: Keep the reason for joining visible
instruction.body: Members who joined for a goal tend to stay longer when it stays visible. Revisit the goal at set points, compare it with progress data, and agree the next step with the member. A general check-in adds little. A specific conversation about the goal shows whether the programme still fits.

instruction.heading: Catch dissatisfaction early
instruction.body: Use short check-ins at about weeks two, six and twelve, and a brief exit form for anyone who stops. Treat each sign of dissatisfaction first as a coaching question: is the programme too easy or too hard, is the member getting enough attention, does the group time suit them? Act on the largest controllable reason first. Booking and package terms are covered in the booking and retention lesson and are not repeated here.

procedure: List each reason a member left in the last six months, with a count.
Mark each reason as controllable or outside your control.
Set check-in dates for each new member.
Act on the largest controllable reason with one specific change.

workedExamples.situation: A hypothetical group of 12 members loses three in one quarter: two say the session time clashes with their work, and one moves interstate.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which reason should the business act on?
workedExamples.reasoning: The move is outside the business's control, so record it without acting on it. The two timing clashes are controllable, so check whether a second session time or a different day is feasible. The decision follows the sorted counts.

commonErrors.error: Treating every departure as a pricing issue
commonErrors.prevention: Sort the reasons first and act on the controllable ones.

commonErrors.error: Stopping check-ins after the first week
commonErrors.prevention: Schedule check-ins at weeks two, six and twelve.

commonErrors.error: Ignoring a quiet member who attends less often
commonErrors.prevention: Flag reduced attendance and check in early.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Retention messages must not rely on health claims or unproven promises; see the claims lesson.
Storing exit feedback is personal information handling.

qualityStandard: Each departure has a recorded and sorted reason
Check-ins are scheduled for every new member
One controllable change is recorded each quarter
summary: Sort reasons into controllable and not controllable.
Check in early and act on the largest controllable reason.

knowledgeChecks.question: Relocation as a reason for leaving a small group is best classed as:
options: A reason to raise the price now

knowledgeChecks.question: Which step keeps a member connected to the reason they joined?
options: Revisiting the goal at set points and comparing it with progress
Stopping check-ins after week one and sending no more messages
Removing goals from the member file and the start date of the plan

knowledgeChecks.question: Why are check-ins scheduled at about weeks two, six and twelve?
